meta.status: Prototype. Labels follow the AI Act text; where the briefing booklet differs, the register says so. Pending review by the D7 owner.
meta.legalBasis: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act) as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI), in force 27 July 2026
sources: European Commission guidelines on prohibited AI practices, on transparency (Art. 50; final, November 2026: reference to confirm, the booklet cites C(2026) 7702 final of 5 Nov 2026, other sources OJ C/2026/6005 of 12 Nov 2026) and draft guidelines on high-risk classification (19 May 2026), as read by the project team
AI Governance for European Hotels, briefing booklet by EHL SBP Group 36 for HFTP (November 2026)
Hotel AI Use-Case Catalogue, 91 use cases in 15 departments (EHL SBP Group 36, 11 November 2026)
Desk research and text check of both regulations by the project team, 17 November 2026
EU AI Act hospitality deep dive (research report, 17 Nov 2026): text check of both regulations and corrections to the booklet

prohibited.name: Prohibited
prohibited.short: Banned. It cannot be made compliant; a narrow exception covers genuine medical or safety reasons.

high.name: High-risk
high.short: On the Act's list of high-risk uses. The maker must test, document, CE-mark and register the tool; the hotel must use it under trained human oversight.

highif.name: High-risk if…
highif.short: The same kind of tool can be set up either way. One feature or one use makes it high-risk: answer the open questions to settle it.

transparency.name: Transparency
transparency.short: People must know they are dealing with AI, or that content is AI-made.

transif.name: Transparency if…
transif.short: A transparency duty applies depending on how the tool is used: answer the open question.

minimal.name: Minimal
minimal.short: No duty under the AI Act beyond AI literacy. Other laws may still apply.

outside.name: Outside the high-risk list
outside.short: The Act excludes this use from its high-risk list, but other law covers it strictly.

notai.name: Not an AI system
notai.short: Software that follows rules written entirely by people is not AI under the Act. Other laws still apply.

open.name: Not labelled yet
open.short: Answer the questions to get a label.

banif.name: Could be banned
banif.short: A question that decides whether this use is banned is still unanswered or "Not sure". Answer it before relying on any lower label.

law.name: Law text
law.desc: Written in the AI Act as amended in July 2026, or a direct application of an article to the hotel use.

guidance.name: Commission guidance
guidance.desc: Final Commission guidelines. Not binding, but the Commission's own reading of the Act.

draft.name: Draft guidance
draft.desc: The Commission's draft guidelines on high-risk AI (19 May 2026). They may change in the final version.

reading.name: Our reading
reading.desc: The project team’s interpretation where neither the law nor Commission guidance gives the answer. Not tested by a regulator or court.

default.name: Law text: not listed
default.desc: Not on the AI Act’s list of prohibited or high-risk uses, and no transparency duty applies. Only AI literacy applies.

duty.name: AI Act duty
duty.desc: A duty the AI Act places on your hotel.

maker.name: Maker's duty, your check
maker.desc: The AI Act places the duty on the tool's maker. Your part is to check it has been done.

law.name: Other law
law.desc: Required by another law that applies to the same tool.

practice.name: Good practice
practice.desc: Not a legal duty today, but the starting point for the duties that follow.

open.name: To find out
open.desc: An answer you marked "Not sure". It can change the label, so find out who can confirm it.

standard.name: Contract / industry standard
standard.desc: Required by a contract or an industry standard, not by law.

tags.Consumer: EU consumer law; UK Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
tags.Liability: Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853; food information rules
tags.Cyber/PCI: Cyber Resilience Act; card-payment standard PCI DSS

emo_staff.q: Does it read the emotions, mood or wellbeing of staff or job candidates from their face or voice?
emo_staff.reason: It reads the emotions of staff or job candidates from face or voice, which is banned at work.
emo_staff.help: Reading the text of reviews or messages does not count. A narrow exception covers genuine medical or safety reasons; staff wellbeing or engagement does not, and staff consent does not either. That job candidates are covered comes from Commission guidance.

coach_emo.q: Does it read a person's emotions from face or voice, with results that reach HR or managers?
coach_emo.reason: The coach reads emotions and the results reach HR or managers.
coach_emo.help: An AI coach may read a person's emotions only if the results stay with that person.

sensitive_traits.q: Does it infer sensitive traits, such as ethnicity, religion or sexual orientation, from how people look?
sensitive_traits.reason: It sorts people by sensitive traits inferred from their appearance.

exploit_price.q: Is pricing or selling designed to deceive or manipulate guests, or to exploit their age, disability or financial situation, in a way that causes significant harm?
exploit_price.reason: It is designed to exploit a guest's age, disability or financial situation and cause significant harm.
exploit_price.help: Demand-based pricing and honest upselling are not affected. "The guest cannot compare prices" is not a vulnerability under the Act; consumer law covers that.

social_score.q: Does it score guests using data from unrelated contexts, such as social media or other operators, and lead to refusing them or treating them worse?
social_score.reason: It scores people on data from unrelated contexts and leads to unfavourable treatment.
social_score.help: A plain do-not-rent list kept by hand is not AI. Disproportionate treatment can be caught even within one property.

rank_staff.q: Does it rank, score or rate individual staff, for example on speed, punctuality, reliability or ratings, or report results per person to supervisors?
rank_staff.reason: It ranks, scores or reports on individual staff.
rank_staff.help: Allocating work only by room status or stated availability does not count (draft guidance). A manager signing off does not take the tool out of high-risk. Switching the feature off does not change the label if the vendor still describes the tool as monitoring staff: ask for a version whose stated purpose excludes it.

hours_leave.q: Does it significantly change regular working hours, or decide leave requests?
hours_leave.reason: It changes regular working hours or decides leave.

career_decide.q: Are its results used to decide pay, promotion, contract renewal or dismissal?
career_decide.reason: Its results are used to decide pay, promotion, renewal or dismissal.
career_decide.help: Letting a fixed-term contract lapse on an AI score counts as ending it.

judge_staff.q: Are its footage, logs or alerts used to rate or judge individual staff?
judge_staff.reason: Its footage, logs or alerts are used to judge individual staff.
judge_staff.help: Reporting results to the team as a whole, not by person, keeps it minimal. Keeping data only for the shift is a data protection measure; it does not change the label.

repurpose_hr.q: Is it used to rank job applicants or to rate or judge staff?
repurpose_hr.reason: A general tool is used to rank applicants or judge staff, which is a high-risk use.
repurpose_hr.help: This applies from 2 Dec 2027. Whether your hotel then becomes the tool's maker is the least settled point in the law (draft guidance). The data protection problem exists today: CVs and staff data go to an outside service.

job_ads.q: Is the same tool used to place targeted job adverts?
job_ads.reason: It places targeted job adverts, which the Act lists under recruitment.

emo_guest.q: Does it read guests' or callers' emotions from their voice or face?
emo_guest.reason: It reads guests' or callers' emotions from voice or face.

voiceprint.q: Does it recognise callers by their voiceprint without their active involvement?
voiceprint.reason: It recognises callers by voiceprint without their active involvement.

face_distance.q: Does it recognise guests or staff at a distance by their face, for example VIP or banned-guest matching on cameras?
face_distance.reason: It recognises people at a distance by their face.
face_distance.help: A guest who steps up to an entry camera to be checked is not 'at a distance'. Face recognition of guests uses biometric data; GDPR Art. 9 almost always requires explicit consent, and an alternative must be offered.

crowd_mood.q: Does it read the mood of crowds or groups?
crowd_mood.reason: It reads the mood of crowds or groups.

safety_part.q: Is the AI part of the safety function of a lift, gas appliance or pressure equipment, for example lift doors or gas combustion control?
safety_part.reason: The AI is part of the safety function of a regulated product.
safety_part.help: Predicting maintenance needs, or optimising energy, comfort or efficiency, is not a safety component unless failure of the AI itself would endanger people. Machinery such as kitchen equipment and robots is covered by machinery law instead.

aggression.q: Does it detect aggression, anger or intentions from people's gestures, face or voice?
aggression.reason: It infers aggression or intentions from people's gestures, face or voice.
aggression.help: Detecting an object, such as a weapon, does not count. Merely detecting a raised voice is not emotion recognition.

bio_categorise.q: Does it analyse guests' skin, face or body to sort them into categories?
bio_categorise.reason: It sorts people into categories from their biometric data, so the people exposed must be told.

med_device.q: Is the product sold as a medical device?
med_device.reason: AI in a medical device is high-risk, and meeting the rules is the maker's duty.

c_staff.q: Does it hire, rank, score, monitor or evaluate staff or job candidates, allocate work based on how they behave, or feed decisions on pay, promotion or ending contracts?
c_staff.reason: It hires, ranks, monitors or evaluates staff or candidates.

c_biometric.q: Does it recognise people at a distance by face or voice, or read guests' emotions?
c_biometric.reason: It recognises people at a distance or reads their emotions.
c_biometric.help: Matching a guest's selfie to their own ID document does not count.

c_credit.q: Does it score how creditworthy an individual guest is?
c_credit.reason: It scores the creditworthiness of individuals.
c_credit.help: Fraud checks do not count: the Act expressly excludes fraud detection here. Ordinary deposits and pre-authorisations are not high-risk on the draft guidance; pay-later schemes, house accounts for individuals and long-stay housing are less clear.

c_chat.q: Does it chat or talk with guests or with staff?
c_chat.reason: It talks to people, so they must be told it is AI.
c_chat.help: Whether a tool is "obviously" AI is judged case by case in the law; the Commission reads it narrowly for guest-facing chat and voice.

auto_reply.q: Does it reply to guests by itself, without a person sending the message?
auto_reply.reason: It replies to guests by itself, so they must be told it is AI.
auto_reply.help: A draft that a person reads and sends is not affected.

robot_talks.q: Does the robot talk with guests in a way that is not obviously a machine?
robot_talks.reason: It talks to guests and is not obviously a machine.
robot_talks.help: Whether a robot is "obviously" a machine is judged case by case in the law.

ai_image.q: Do you publish realistic AI-made images, video or audio that could pass for real, for example of the hotel, its food or its staff, including voice clones, avatars or dubbed videos?
ai_image.reason: Realistic AI-made media that could mislead must be labelled.
ai_image.help: A real photo with minor edits needs no label. An AI label does not make a misleading picture lawful under consumer law.

staff_likeness.q: Is the avatar or voice a likeness of a real employee?
staff_likeness.reason: A likeness of a real person made with AI must be disclosed.
staff_likeness.help: The employee's consent does not replace the disclosure.

pub_claims.q: Do you publish AI-written claims about health, safety or sustainability without a person checking them first?
pub_claims.reason: AI-written text on matters of public interest, published without human review, must be disclosed.

card_data.q: Do card numbers pass through it, spoken on a call or typed into a chat?
card_data.help: This does not change the AI Act label, but it brings the tool under the card-payment security standard.

personal_price.q: Is any price or offer personalised from a guest's profile or behaviour?
personal_price.help: This does not change the AI Act label. Demand-based prices that are the same for everyone need no notice.

competitor_data.q: Does it use other hotels' non-public data, or share your prices with them?
competitor_data.help: This does not change the AI Act label, but competing hotels feeding the same tool can amount to price coordination.

scan_staff.q: Does it scan staff email or staff activity?
scan_staff.help: This does not change the AI Act label, but tools that scan staff email are staff monitoring too (our reading).

paste_data.q: Do staff paste guest or staff personal data into it?
paste_data.help: This does not change the AI Act label. A paste sends personal data to an outside service; that can be a data breach.

face_enrol.q: Does it build a face recognition database from everyone captured on your cameras?
face_enrol.reason: It builds a face database by untargeted scraping of camera footage, which is banned.
face_enrol.help: Matching against a list of specific people who agreed to be enrolled is a different case.

crime_profile.q: Does it predict whether a guest will commit an offence based only on their profile or personal traits?
crime_profile.reason: It predicts offences from a profile alone, which is banned.
crime_profile.help: Alerts based on what someone actually does, or on the transaction itself, are not affected.

academy.q: Is it used in a hotel school or training academy to admit learners, assess their results or monitor them in tests?
academy.reason: It assesses learners in education or vocational training.
academy.help: Whether an in-company academy counts as a vocational training institution is not settled.

items.text: Check whether the banned feature can be switched off. If it cannot, stop using the tool.
items.note: Fines for banned practices go up to €35m or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (AI Act Art. 99(3)).

items.text: Check whether the tool says it is AI at the start of each conversation or call. A line in the terms and conditions is not enough.
items.ref: AI Act Art. 50(1) (maker's duty); EU consumer law
items.note: The law puts this duty on the tool's maker (Art. 50(1)), not on a hotel that uses a vendor's tool. Checking it is still sensible, and a hidden bot can breach consumer law.

items.text: Check whether your group's tool says it is AI at the start of each conversation or call: as its maker, the group owes this itself.
Check whether each realistic AI-made image, video or audio clip that could pass for real (the hotel, its food or its staff, including voice clones, avatars and dubbed videos) carries a label.
items.note: A real photo with minor edits needs no label. Where an agency makes the content and decides how it uses AI, the agency labels it. The Commission-backed Code of Practice on marking and labelling AI content (June 2026) gives label templates.

items.text: Check whether the hotel's marketing uses AI images that show something the hotel does not have. A label does not make a misleading picture lawful.
Check whether a person reviews AI-written claims about health, safety or sustainability before they are published. If not, the text must say it is AI-written.
items.ref: AI Act Art. 50(4); Commission transparency guidelines

items.text: Check whether the people exposed are told that the system reads emotions or sorts people by a biometric trait.
Check whether the tool is used as the maker's instructions for use say.
Check whether trained staff are named to oversee the tool, with the authority to overrule it.
Check whether the tool's logs are kept for at least six months, where they are under your control.
items.note: Only the logs the hotel actually controls, or can obtain from the vendor under the contract.

items.text: Check whether staff and their representatives are told before the tool is used on them.

Check whether people (staff, candidates or guests) are told when the tool is used in decisions about them, and whether you can explain on request its role in a decision with a significant negative effect.
Check whether you can suspend the tool, and tell the vendor and the authority, if it may put people's health, safety or rights at risk.
Check whether someone can answer the authorities' questions about the tool.
Check with the vendor whether the tool is a legacy tool or will be CE-marked and registered by 2 Dec 2027, and ask to be told before an update changes that.
items.note: Not a legal duty on a private hotel, but you need the answer. A tool already in use before 2 Dec 2027 stays outside these duties, for the vendor and for your hotel, until its design changes significantly. That later purchases of the same model are covered rests on a recital only, and cloud tools that keep updating are unlikely to keep this status.

items.text: Check whether the tool has been tested, documented, checked against the rules, CE-marked and registered before use: your group is its maker. This is specialist work: get legal and technical support.
You may be treated as the provider of this tool, because you use a general tool for a high-risk purpose (AI Act Art. 25(1)(c)). Get legal advice, and check whether the vendor's terms forbid this use.
Check whether the group follows EN 18286:2026, the harmonised standard for the quality-management system.
Check with the maker whether the product carries the CE mark for its AI safety function. Meeting the high-risk rules is the maker's duty from 2 Aug 2028.

Check whether design and testing records are kept. AI that a group builds for its own use and puts into use after 9 Dec 2026 is a product it manufactures; without records the group is in a weaker position if a defect is alleged.
Check whether the output of any image or text generator the group builds or adapts carries a machine-readable AI mark. Generators placed on the market before 2 Aug 2026 must comply by 2 Dec 2026.
Take measures so that staff and contractors who use this tool understand what it does and where it can go wrong (for example a short briefing), and keep a note.
items.note: AI Act Art. 4 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (in force 27 Jul 2026). No certificate or specific level is required. From 2 Dec 2027 the staff overseeing high-risk tools must be competent.

items.text: Check whether one person in the hotel is named as responsible for this tool.
Check whether the vendor has answered the questions below, and whether the answers are in the contract.
Check whether the works council or staff representatives, where you have them, are involved before this tool is introduced or changed.

items.who: General manager, with the data protection officer
items.text: Check whether a data protection impact assessment has been done before the tool is switched on.

Check whether the tool alone makes decisions about a person that have legal or similarly significant effects. If it does, the person must be able to get a human review, to give their view and to contest the decision.
Check whether guests give explicit consent, are offered a check-in without face scanning, and whether no central store of guests' face templates is kept (our reading).
Check whether staff have a real non-biometric alternative to the time clock. The Spanish data protection authority (AEPD) considers biometric time clocks unlawful in most cases.
Check whether ID document scans are kept only as long as they are needed.
Check whether personalisation from guest data, which is profiling, has a legal basis and whether guests are told about it.
Check whether marketing emails go only to people who consented, or to existing customers for similar services with an easy opt-out.
Check whether body, skin and sleep data are treated as health data: explicit consent, and only what the treatment needs.
Check whether staff have an approved AI tool with a work account, and know not to paste guest or staff personal data into personal chatbots.

Check whether there is a written security agreement with the vendor and card numbers are kept out of recordings and chats. Card data brings the tool under the card industry's security standard (PCI DSS).
items.ref: PCI DSS (card industry standard, applied through contracts)

items.text: Check whether a notice before each booking says the price is personalised. A line in the privacy policy is not enough.
Check whether any AI-written review could be published as genuine.
Check whether the tool feeds your prices to competing hotels or bases your rates on their non-public data.
Check whether a person reviews allergen information before guests see it: it stays the hotel's responsibility whatever tool produces it.
Check, when buying connected equipment, whether it carries the CE mark now, and from 11 Dec 2027 whether the maker can prove it meets the Cyber Resilience Act.

items.who: General manager, with the brand or head office
items.text: Check whether the franchise or management agreement says who carries which duty for this tool. The brand or head office chose it, so the brand may also be a user (deployer) of it, or its provider if the tool carries the brand's name.
items.note: Our reading: which party is the deployer depends on who uses the tool under its authority; the contract should say so.

labourNotes.DE: Germany: the works council co-decides on tools able to monitor staff, and a rollout that skips this step can be stopped.
labourNotes.FR: France: consult the staff committee (CSE) in firms of 50 or more. Approving a chatbot staff already use also counts as introducing it.
labourNotes.ES: Spain: every employer using algorithms on staff must also inform each worker individually.
labourNotes.SE: Sweden: negotiate with the union before an important change to working conditions.
labourNotes.CH: Switzerland: systems meant to monitor staff behaviour are banned. Proportionate performance monitoring is allowed with staff involved in planning it.
labourNotes.GB: United Kingdom: human involvement counts only if a trained person with authority reviews each decision; spot checks are not enough (regulator's draft guidance).

vendorQuestions.q: Who is the maker of this tool under the AI Act, and does the contract say so?
Does it rank, score or monitor individual staff, read emotions, or recognise people by face or voice? Can those features be switched off?
Is the 'you are talking to AI' notice built in and switched on?
Where is the data stored, and will you sign a data processing agreement? If data leaves the EU, on what legal basis?
Will you supply instructions for use and logs, and have the tool CE-marked and registered before 2 Dec 2027? Will you tell us before an update changes what the tool does?
Do you train your models on our data or our guests' data, and can we opt out?
Do your pricing or revenue recommendations use other hotels' non-public data, or share ours with them?

origins.name: Bought from a vendor and used as supplied
Came inside a system we already had (PMS, CRM, phone system)
Switched on by a vendor update
Built by or for our group, under our own name
A vendor's tool with our name on it
A vendor's tool we changed substantially, for example retrained on our data

build.name: Build it
build.text: Your group developed the tool and uses it under its own name, so the group is its maker.

brand.name: Brand it
brand.text: Putting your name on a vendor's high-risk tool makes your group its maker.

change.name: Change it
change.text: Substantially modifying a vendor's high-risk tool makes your group its maker (our reading for retraining on your own data).

repurpose.name: Repurpose it
repurpose.text: From 2 Dec 2027, using a general tool for a high-risk job the vendor did not offer it for may make your hotel its maker. This is the least settled point in the law (draft guidance).

operatingModels.name: Managed
operatingModels.user: The management company, which chooses and runs the tools
operatingModels.watch: Possibly the brand too, where its standards impose a tool and how it is used (our reading). On the wording of the law the user is whoever actually uses the tool; a brand that only imposes it may count as a distributor instead. The owner usually is not, unless it decides on the tools.

operatingModels.name: Franchised
operatingModels.user: The franchisee, which runs the hotel
operatingModels.watch: Possibly the brand too, where franchise standards impose a tool and its settings (our reading). On the wording of the law the user is whoever actually uses the tool; a brand that only imposes it may count as a distributor instead.

operatingModels.name: Leased
operatingModels.user: The tenant who operates the hotel

hotelChecks.text: Check whether every guest chatbot and phone agent says it is AI at the start of the conversation.
hotelChecks.note: The law puts this duty on the tool's maker; if your group built the tool, the group owes it directly (Art. 50(1), since 2 Aug 2026). For a vendor's tool it is a sensible check and protects against consumer-law claims.

diff.booklet: "Required since 2 Aug 2026" for every hotel (Start here, item 1).
diff.law: Art. 50(1) binds providers. A hotel using a vendor's bot owes it only if it is the provider.

hotelChecks.text: Check with HR and department heads whether anyone pastes CVs or staff data into a general chatbot to rank or judge people. If so, stop it.
hotelChecks.note: From 2 Dec 2027 ranking applicants is a high-risk use. Today the problem is data protection law: the paste sends personal data to an outside service.

diff.booklet: States the high-risk and maker risk in the present tense (Start here, item 2).
diff.law: Arts. 6 and 25 apply only from 2 Dec 2027.

hotelChecks.who: Department heads, with IT or purchasing
hotelChecks.text: Check with the vendors of rota, housekeeping, call-centre and camera tools whether they rank individual staff, read emotions or recognise people by face or voice. Switch off what you do not need.
hotelChecks.note: Reading staff emotions has been banned since 2 Feb 2025. Ranking staff and recognising people at a distance become high-risk on 2 Dec 2027.

hotelChecks.who: General manager; head office pools the lists
hotelChecks.text: Check whether every AI tool in use is listed: what it does, who supplies it, who in the hotel is responsible.
hotelChecks.note: This register is that list. It is the starting point for every other duty.

hotelChecks.text: Take measures so that staff and contractors who use AI understand what each tool does and where it can go wrong (for example a short briefing), and keep a note.
hotelChecks.note: AI Act Art. 4 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (in force 27 Jul 2026). No certificate or specific level is required.

CH.reach: A stand-alone Swiss hotel is probably not covered by the EU AI Act for on-site use (our reading). It can be covered where its AI output is used in the EU, for example a chatbot answering guests in the EU (AI Act Art. 2(1)(c)), and any group hotel in the EU is covered. AI Act items below are shown for reference. The Swiss Data Protection Act (revFADP) and labour law apply to AI directly.

items.text: Tell guests and staff when they deal with AI and when a decision is automated, and offer human review.
Check every AI vendor that receives personal data: its security, and the legal basis for data leaving Switzerland.
Write the group's AI policy and involve staff before introducing any tool that monitors them.

Check whether any decision about a person is made by a tool alone with legal effects or a significant impact. If so, the person must be told and be able to give their view and ask for a human review (revFADP Art. 21).

GB.reach: A stand-alone UK hotel is probably not covered by the EU AI Act for on-site use (our reading). It can be covered where its AI output is used in the EU, for example a chatbot answering guests in the EU (AI Act Art. 2(1)(c)), and any group hotel in the EU is covered. AI Act items below are shown for reference. UK GDPR, consumer and employment law apply to AI directly.

items.text: For any decision made by machine alone about applicants, staff pay or shifts, or guest refusals: tell the people affected, let them contest it, and name a trained person who can change it.
Use biometric check-in or clock-ins only with explicit consent and a real non-biometric alternative.
Show the total price upfront and never publish AI-written reviews as genuine.
